title: Time Traveller
intro: Present perfect or past simple? The difference that catches out almost every Spanish speaker.

A2.why: “Last year” is a finished time: past simple.

A2.q: I ___ sushi many times in my life.
A2.why: “In my life” is still going on, and the exact times don’t matter: present perfect.

A2.q: She ___ her keys. She can't find them.
A2.why: The keys are still missing now: present perfect for a past action with a result today.
“Yesterday evening” is finished and stated: past simple.
“Since 2020” runs up to now: present perfect, not “lives” as in Spanish “vive desde”.
“An hour ago” points to a finished moment: past simple.
“Finished” plus “yet” in a question needs “have”: present perfect.
“Last month” is a finished time: past simple.
“Has just” needs the past participle: arrived.
“In 2019” is a stated past date: past simple.

A2.q: My grandmother ___ in Valencia all her life — she still lives in the same street.
A2.why: “All her life” and she still lives there: present perfect.

A2.q: The sheriff ___ the bank robbers two days ago.
A2.why: “Two days ago” is a finished time: past simple.

B1.q: It’s only ten o’clock, and I ___ three cups of coffee so far this morning.
B1.why: “So far this morning” counts up to now: present perfect.

B1.q: She ___ to Japan twice so far.
B1.why: “So far” counts experiences up to now: present perfect, with “been to” for a trip there and back.
“Last Friday” is a finished time: past simple.

B1.q: He ___ his car since he got his licence.
B1.why: “Since he got his licence” runs up to now: present perfect.

B1.q: ___ you see Maria at the party last night?
B1.why: “Last night” is finished, so the question uses “did”.

B1.q: I ___ my keys this morning — I still can't find them.
B1.why: “I still can’t find them” is the result now: present perfect.

B1.q: They ___ married for ten years now.
B1.why: “For ten years now” runs up to today: present perfect, not “are” as in Spanish.
“In 2018” is a stated past date: past simple.

B1.q: I ___ never seen such a beautiful place.
B1.why: “Never seen” is your whole life up to now: have + past participle.

B1.q: We ___ here for six months now.
B1.why: “For six months now” runs up to today: present perfect, not “live”.

B1.q: Penicillin ___ millions of lives since Fleming discovered it.
B1.why: “Since Fleming discovered it” runs up to now: present perfect.
“In 1965” is a stated past date: past simple.

B2.q: I ___ him so far today — maybe he’s ill.
B2.why: “So far today” means the day isn’t over: present perfect.

B2.q: ___ you finished the report? The deadline was an hour ago.
B2.why: “Finished” after the gap needs “have”: the report matters now.

B2.q: This week ___ very busy so far.
B2.why: “This week” isn’t over and “so far” counts up to now: present perfect.

B2.q: He ___ his job last week — he's now unemployed.
B2.why: “Last week” is finished and stated, even though the result is now: past simple.

B2.q: I ___ that film three times now.
B2.why: “Three times now” counts experiences up to today: present perfect.

B2.q: She ___ to five countries so far this year.
B2.why: “So far this year” is an unfinished period: present perfect.

B2.q: We ___ any news from the lab since Monday.
B2.why: “Since Monday” runs up to now: present perfect.
“Already” with a result now (“don’t worry”): present perfect.
“Ever” plus “lived” asks about her life up to now: “has”.

B2.q: The company ___ three new products since January.
B2.why: “Since January” runs up to now: present perfect.

B2.q: The old cowboy ___ a horse since his accident in the 1990s.
B2.why: “Since his accident” runs up to now: present perfect.

B2.q: When I was a child, my family ___ to the Fallas every March.
B2.why: “When I was a child” is a finished period: past simple.

C1.q: This is the first time I ___ Japanese food.
C1.why: “This is the first time” is always followed by the present perfect in English.

C1.q: It’s the best film I ___ for years.
C1.why: A superlative plus “for years” up to now: present perfect.

C1.q: I can't believe how much the city ___ since I last visited.
C1.why: “Since I last visited” runs up to now: present perfect.

C1.q: She ___ several awards so far in her career.
C1.why: “So far” tells us her career is still going: present perfect.

C1.q: We ___ the contract last Tuesday, so it's now legally binding.
C1.why: “Last Tuesday” is a stated past time: past simple, even with a result now.

C1.q: Prices ___ steadily since 2015, and there’s no sign of a slowdown.
C1.why: “Since 2015” runs up to now: present perfect.

C1.q: He ___ his resignation this morning at nine o'clock.
C1.why: “At nine o’clock” pins down the moment: past simple.

C1.q: It ___ the hottest summer on record so far.
C1.why: “So far” measures up to now: present perfect.

C1.q: The government ___ new regulations last year, and they remain in force.
C1.why: “Last year” is finished and stated: past simple.

C1.q: Sales ___ significantly since the new website launched.
C1.why: “Since the new website launched” runs up to now: present perfect.

C1.q: Ever since Jenner’s first vaccine, doctors ___ that prevention is better than cure.
C1.why: “Ever since” stretches from then up to now: present perfect.

C1.q: The last stagecoach ___ through the town over a century ago, but the old inn still stands.
C1.why: “Over a century ago” is finished: past simple, even though the inn is still there.
